processing: A cultivar rather than one style: mostly steamed and rolled into sencha, and also shade-grown and ground into matcha by some producers.
harvest_season: Buds slightly early; spring first flush is the usual choice, as with other Japanese single-cultivar teas.
appearance_dry: As sencha, deep green needles; the fresh young leaf is elliptical, thin, soft and yellow-green.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green when made as sencha.
appearance_wet: Soft, thin green leaf, typical of a tender sencha.
taste_profile: Rich and savoury with balanced sweetness, and an aroma that is noticeably different from Yabukita.

brewing.notes: Usual sencha settings. Cooler water keeps the savouriness forward and holds the aroma.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring sencha, usually named as a single cultivar or blended with one such as Saemidori. As with other sencha, drink it within the year; it is not an ageing tea.
description:
Asanoka is a Japanese tea cultivar whose name is often translated as morning fragrance. It is grown mostly in Kagoshima, and it matters to tea drinkers because it offers a different aroma from the Yabukita that fills most Japanese fields.

It is largely made into sencha, though it also appears as matcha. Single-origin versions turn up beyond Kagoshima as well, in places such as Wazuka in Kyoto and the Ohmi area.

Expect a rich, savoury cup with sweetness balancing it and an aroma tasters mark as unlike Yabukita. Standard sencha brewing works: about 70 °C and a minute for the first steep, then a quick second one.

It is easy to find as a single-cultivar sencha from specialist Japanese tea shops, and in blends with Saemidori. Buy the most recent spring harvest. If you enjoy it, taste it next to a Yabukita to see what the cultivar itself brings.
history:
Asanoka was bred in Kagoshima by crossing Yabukita with a parent from China, and it was officially registered in 1996. Accounts differ on that Chinese parent, naming it CP1 or Hiramizu No. 1, and the matter remains unsettled.

It has stayed largely a Kagoshima cultivar, valued for its slightly early budding, cold hardiness and high yield.
